cases.title: Profitable OEM instrument maker, temporary dip, leverage 2.1x, family stake 31%
reasons: Segment fit: OEM analyzer systems fall within the in-vitro diagnostics segments we like (OEM analyzers). Outside-segment rule does not apply.
Business model: consumables and service are 62% of sales, above the 50% recurring-revenue threshold. No warning. Multi-year OEM supply contracts add visibility.
Profitability: EBITDA margin is 17% LTM, so the company is profitable. Market cap of EUR 420m is mid-sized.

Why the price is low: the 38% drop over 12 months is tied to a two-quarter slip in the new analyzer platform launch. That is a product-transition delay, which the thesis counts as temporary. It is not a loss of market. The H1 release shows order intake recovering and the first platform shipments done, which supports the view that the cause is fading. The 3-month change of -6% shows the decline has slowed.

Kill criteria, none met: (1) Net debt/EBITDA is 2.1x from the data, below the 4x limit. (2) The controlling holder has made no public statement about its stake, so there is no ruling out of a sale. (3) No regulatory matters are reported.

Ownership flag: the founding family (Northline Beteiligungen) holds 31%, above the 25% threshold. No public statement about selling, so this is a flag only. It is not a reject. The family's position is unknown, and that is the key diligence point. A take-private needs their support. But the thesis treats a founding family with a large stake as a feature of a good fit, and an unknown stance does not trigger a kill criterion.

Thesis match: this closely mirrors the 'good fit' example: a profitable OEM instrument maker with long supply contracts, a share price down sharply after a product transition, and a founding family with a large stake.

Caveat: Priority is not Actionable. Actionable is granted by code only if the takeout price is at or below the target price. Next steps are to sound out the family's intentions and to check that platform ramp-up is on track.

cases.title: Same profile as a clean fit, but net debt at 3.9x EBITDA
reasons: Segment fit: immunoassay instruments and reagents are in-vitro diagnostics, a segment we like. Reagents and service are 70% of sales, above the 50% recurring-revenue bar. Profitable, with an EBITDA margin of 19%.

Price drop looks temporary: shares are down 29% over 12 months because of a one-off inventory write-down tied to the integration of the acquisition. That matches the thesis case of a one-off charge, not a structural loss of market. Note that the facts do not say whether sales or share are holding up after the write-down.
Ownership: no holder above 25%. The largest is Amundi at 7%, and insiders hold 8%. No flag and no sale-related statements. No regulatory issue.

Kill criterion: net debt/EBITDA is 3.9x per the data, below the 4x threshold. No kill criterion is met, so this is not a Reject. The margin is only 0.1x, which is thin. The leverage is also recent, from a debt-financed acquisition, and the 3x deleveraging target within 18 months is only a management guidance, not an achieved fact.

Why not Priority: the rule says an unknown fact is never a pass. The temporary nature of the drop and the path to lower leverage both rest on management statements and on integration risk. Nothing independent confirms that the write-down is truly one-off or that the acquisition is performing. The leverage cushion is too small to treat the kill criterion as safely cleared. The company also needs to absorb the integration without a further charge or an EBITDA miss, because either would push leverage above 4x.
Why not Reject: the 4x kill threshold is not breached, no controlling shareholder exists, and no regulatory issue is reported.

Conclusion: this is a strong strategic fit (IVD, recurring revenue, temporary drop) that should stay on the Radar. It should move to Priority once there is evidence that the write-down is one-off (clean results after integration), that leverage is falling toward 3x, and that the acquired business is performing. It should move to Reject if leverage crosses 4x.

reasons: Segment fits. Vireo Analytics makes OEM analyzer systems and lab automation for IVD companies, which is explicitly one of the segments we like.
Business model passes. Service and consumables are 55% of sales, above the 50% threshold, so the warning does not trigger. The margin is thin at 12% EBITDA, but the company is profitable.

The 21% rebound in the last quarter after a strong Q2 release supports that. The 12-month change is still -15%, so there is room left. This is the least certain point: the destocking is attributed to a single customer, and customer concentration is worth checking in diligence.

Fit with the thesis examples: this is close to the stated good fit, a profitable OEM instrument and automation maker with supply relationships, a share price hit by a customer-driven setback, and a founding family holding a large stake.

cases.title: Profitable, cheap, but the market is going away
reasons: No kill criterion is met. Net debt/EBITDA is 0.4x, well under the 4x limit (taken from the data, not computed). There is no holder above 25% (top holder Vanguard at 9%, insiders 4%), so the ownership rule has nothing to flag and nobody has ruled out a sale. No regulatory issue is reported. This is therefore not a Reject.

The company fails the 'why the price is low' criterion. The thesis requires a temporary cause such as a product transition, customer destocking or a one-off charge, and says structural decline goes to Radar. Here revenue has fallen three years in a row as pandemic testing volumes disappear. The latest release shows a further 30% decline. That is demand normalising after a one-time spike, not a temporary dip.

Management has no new product with meaningful sales. The thesis's good-fit example is a share price that is down sharply after a product transition, and there is no transition and no replacement revenue to point to. The 62% fall over 12 months, with a further 18% over 3 months, matches continuing erosion of the revenue base, not a one-off event.

The segment fits. Rapid antigen tests are in-vitro diagnostics and the company is profitable (24% EBITDA margin). But the margin comes from cost cuts on a shrinking top line, so it is not a sign of a healthy franchise, and the strategy depends on the decline being temporary.

The recurring revenue share (consumables and service at 50% of sales or more) is not stated in the facts. This is a warning only, not a reject. Antigen tests are mostly single-use, but the facts do not give a recurring share, and an unknown fact is never a pass.

Verdict: Radar, not Reject, because no kill criterion is met, and not Priority, because the drop looks structural. It would move toward Priority only if evidence emerged of a credible product pipeline or stabilising revenue. Without that it should stay on watch with low conviction, and the code should not grant Actionable status.

cases.title: Good company, wrong segment: medical imaging equipment
reasons: Segment mismatch: Lumen Imaging makes ultrasound and point-of-care imaging systems. That is medical imaging, not in-vitro diagnostics (instruments, assays, OEM analyzers, lab automation). The thesis rule says outside these segments the verdict is Radar. This is the decisive criterion.

Kill criteria are not met, so this is not a Reject. Net debt/EBITDA is 1.8x against the 4x limit (figure taken from the data). The facts report no regulatory issue. There is no controlling shareholder: the top holder, Baillie Gifford, owns 11%, insiders own 6%, and no holder is above 25%, so the ownership flag is not triggered.

Business model gives a warning only. Service contracts are 40% of sales, below the 50% recurring-revenue bar. The thesis says this is never a reject, but it adds to the case for not making this a Priority. The facts do not say how much of the rest is consumables, so recurring revenue may be somewhat higher.

The price drop looks temporary, which fits the thesis. The 12-month fall of -33% is attributed to a delayed UK hospital tender cycle that management expects to resume. That is a timing issue, not a structural loss of market. It is still management's expectation and we have not verified it. The 3-month move of -7% shows the stock has not recovered. We should track whether tenders actually resume.
Profitability and size are acceptable: a 16% EBITDA margin and a €900m market cap, so the company is profitable and mid-sized. This is not enough to override the segment rule.

Conclusion: Radar. Keep watching, because the quality, leverage and temporary-drop profile is attractive. It does not qualify as Priority because it is outside the IVD segments and recurring revenue is below half of sales. Revisit if the fund widens the segment scope to include imaging, or if the service share and tender recovery are confirmed.

reasons: Segment fit: Lab automation systems fall within the in-vitro diagnostics segments we like (instruments, assays, OEM analyzers, lab automation). No segment issue.

The recurring-revenue criterion is clearly missed (20% vs 50%), and the strategy is built on recurring revenue (consumables, service, supply contracts). Capital equipment sales are also cyclical and lumpy, which is exactly what caused the order delays. Under the thesis, 'a thesis criterion is not met' maps to Radar, not Reject, because the business-model rule is warning-only.

cases.title: Drop blamed on temporary destocking, but a major customer is also insourcing
reasons: Segment fit: immunoassay reagents and instruments is in-vitro diagnostics, a segment we like. No segment-based downgrade.
Business model: reagents and service are 75% of sales, above the 50% recurring-revenue bar. No warning.

Kill criteria: none met. Net debt/EBITDA is 2.0x, below the 4x limit (figure taken from the data, not computed). There is no holder above 25% (top holder Vanguard at 8%, insiders at 6%), so no controlling shareholder has ruled out a sale. There is no regulatory issue.
Ownership rule: no holder above 25%, so there is nothing to flag. Also nothing is known about a sale stance, which is neutral here.

Why the price is low: this is the deciding issue. Management attributes the 35% 12-month fall (18% over 3 months) to temporary customer destocking. That is a company claim, and it fits our 'temporary' categories. But in the same quarter the second-largest customer, a US reference lab network worth about 15% of sales, announced it will move these tests to its own in-house platform from 2027. That is a structural, permanent loss of volume on the installed base, and it is not temporary. The thesis requires the drop to be temporary and says 'Structural decline: Radar'. The two causes are mixed, and the facts do not say how much of the drop or of the profit warning comes from destocking versus the announced customer loss.

Unknown facts are never a pass. We do not know whether the profit warning already reflects the 15% customer loss, whether the in-house move is a full or partial transfer, or whether the destocking is real and measurable. Management's framing also leaves out the customer loss, so we should not rely on it.

Why not Priority: the 'temporary' criterion is not clearly met because a structural revenue loss of about 15% of sales is confirmed. Reagent revenue on installed analyzers is exactly what the customer is moving away from, which also hurts the recurring-revenue model that attracted us.

Why not Reject: no kill criterion is met. Leverage is low, there is no controlling holder, and there is no regulatory issue. The business fits the strategy (profitable, 16% EBITDA margin, recurring revenue, moderate leverage).

What would move it to Priority: evidence that the profit warning and the share price drop are mainly destocking, and that the 2027 loss of the reference lab network is modest and already priced in (for example, a customer-by-customer revenue bridge and guidance that includes the loss), with remaining contracts and new wins offsetting it. Evidence that the loss is larger or spreads to other lab networks would argue for dropping it from the radar.
